facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus was a small ankylosaurian dinosaur that lived in Australia during the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Kunbarrasaurus (meaning "shield lizard") is an extinct genus of small ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Australia.

facts.statement: The first skeleton of Kunbarrasaurus was discovered in November 1989 at Marathon Station near Richmond, Queensland.
facts.quote: In November 1989, at Marathon Station near Richmond, Queensland, the skeleton was discovered of an ankylosaurian.

facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus ieversi was formally named and described in 2015 by a team including Lucy G. Leahey and Ralph E. Molnar.
facts.quote: In 2015, Lucy G. Leahey, Ralph E. Molnar, Kenneth Carpenter, Lawrence M. Witmer and Steven W. Salisbury named and described the type species Kunbarrasaurus ieversi.

facts.statement: The genus name Kunbarrasaurus comes from the Mayi word 'Kunbarra', meaning 'shield'.
facts.quote: The genus name is derived from Kunbarra - the word for 'shield' in the Mayi language of the local Wunumara people.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen QM F1801 was found in the Allaru Formation, dating to the late Albian or possibly early Cenomanian.
facts.quote: The holotype, QM F1801, was found in a layer of the Allaru Formation, marine sediments dating from the late Albian, or possibly the early Cenomanian.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of an almost complete skeleton including the skull, vertebral column up to the middle tail, shoulder girdle, arm, pelvis, thighbones, and most of the body armour.
facts.quote: It consists of an almost complete skeleton with skull, containing the vertebral column up to the middle tail, the left shoulder girdle, the left arm minus the hand, the pelvis, both thighbones and most of the body armour.

facts.statement: Remains of the animal's last meal were preserved in the belly region of the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: In the belly region remains have been found of the animal's last meal.

facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus was a small, quadrupedal, armoured dinosaur estimated to be 2.5 to 3.5 meters long.
facts.quote: Kunbarrasaurus was a small quadrupedal armoured dinosaur. Its length has been estimated at 2.5 - 3.5 m.

facts.statement: The skull roof of Kunbarrasaurus is almost perfectly flat, except for limited convexity in the postorbital and nasal bones.
facts.quote: The roof of the skull is almost perfectly flat, apart from a limited convex profile of the postorbital bone and the nasal bone.

facts.statement: The supraorbital bone in Kunbarrasaurus consists of a single bone rather than two or three.
facts.quote: The supraorbital is made up of one bone instead of two or three.

facts.statement: The side of the braincase was largely cartilage, forcing many brain nerves to exit through a single large opening.
facts.quote: The side of the braincase largely consists of cartilage instead of bone, so that many brain nerves must have had their exits in a single large opening, rather than separate small ones.

facts.statement: The inner ear was very large and unique among dinosaurs, with the vestibule not separated from the brain cavity, a non-bony cochlear floor, and shortened semicircular canals.
facts.quote: The inner ear is very large compared with the skull as a whole and differs from that of all other known Dinosauria in the ear vestibule not being separated from the brain cavity, the floor for the cochlea not being made of bone and the vestibule being so large that the semicircular canals are shortened.

facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus possessed bony body armour covering its head, back, abdomen, legs, and tail.
facts.quote: Kunbarrasaurus had bony protrusions, also known as body armour, in the skin on its head, back, abdomen, legs and along the tail.

facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus had diverse armour including small ossicles, keeled scutes on the body and neck, non-keeled scutes on the snout, spike-like scutes on the hips, and triangular plates on the tail.
facts.quote: Several types of armour are known in place in Kunbarrasaurus, including small ossicles, small keeled scutes on the body ordered in parallel longitudinal rows, large scutes without keels on the snout, large keeled scutes on the neck, shoulders, and possibly tail, spike-like scutes on the hips, and a combination of ridged and keeled scutes and triangular plates on the tail.

facts.statement: A preserved ring of scutes was found around the neck of Kunbarrasaurus.
facts.quote: There was one preserved ring of scutes around the neck.

facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus was a herbivore, like other ankylosaurians.
facts.quote: As with other ankylosaurians, Kunbarrasaurus was herbivorous.

facts.statement: Unlike most herbivorous dinosaurs, direct evidence of Kunbarrasaurus's diet exists in the form of gut contents found in the holotype.
facts.quote: Unlike most herbivorous dinosaurs, there is direct evidence of the diet of Kunbarrasaurus: gut contents are known from the well-preserved nearly complete holotype specimen, found in the abdominal cavity in front of the left ilium.

facts.statement: Clean cuts on plant fragments and the lack of gastroliths suggest Kunbarrasaurus used oral processing rather than stomach stones to grind food.
facts.quote: The clean cuts and lack of gastroliths suggest that the animal relied on oral processing instead of gastroliths or grit to grind food.

facts.statement: In 2021, analysis placed Kunbarrasaurus in the basal Southern Hemisphere lineage Parankylosauria.
facts.quote: In 2021, Sergio Soto-Acuña et al. found Kunbarrasaurus to belong to a distinctive basal lineage of Southern Hemisphere ankylosaurs, the Parankylosauria.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses suggest Kunbarrasaurus is the sister taxon to the clade containing Stegouros and Antarctopelta.
facts.quote: Their phylogenetic analyses placed it as the sister taxon to the clade formed by the Late Cretaceous Stegouros and Antarctopelta.

facts.statement: Kunbarrasaurus lived between 106.3 and 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (106.3 to 100.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is debated whether a 2022 specimen from Warra Station belongs to Kunbarrasaurus leversi, as its authors noted it lacked unique features shared with the type specimen.
facts.quote: In 2022, a specimen collected in 2005 by Benjamin P. Kear from Warra Station near Boulia, Queensland, SAMA P40536 was described and referred to Kunbarrasaurus. However, the describing authors refrained from referring it to K. leversi because it did not share any unique features with the type specimen.
